title: Zero-Carbon Hydrogen Burner for Domestic Heating
summary: Led a team designing a novel hydrogen burner, and led the CFD model that predicted stable hydrogen combustion when hydrogen testing was not possible.

sections.heading: What I did
body: I led a multidisciplinary team through the full design lifecycle: concept generation, design requirements, prototyping, testing and validation. The project was graded 72%.
I built the CFD model in ANSYS Fluent using RANS k-omega SST turbulence and GRI-Mech 3.0 finite-rate chemistry. Teammates adopted the workflow for their own simulations.

sections.heading: Method
body: Polyhedral meshes with wall-resolved inflation layers and local refinement. Mesh independence was shown at 2.3 million cells, using a periodic radial slice to keep the computational cost down.
The model was validated against cold-flow and reactive methane experiments before being extended to hydrogen.

sections.heading: Result
body: The model traced missing outer-ring flames to ambient air dilution. A quartz shield then corrected this and gave a uniform flame.
The validated model predicted stable hydrogen combustion at 8.2 kW and equivalence ratio 0.4 with no flashback.
I also used CNC machining to make prototype components, after evaluating manufacturing processes and joining methods against operating conditions and failure modes.

title: NACA 0012 Airfoil RANS Analysis
summary: A 2D steady RANS study from -11 to +15 degrees angle of attack, validated against NASA data, with a clear account of where and why drag disagreed.

sections.heading: What I did
body: I ran lift and drag polars across the angle-of-attack range and estimated near-stall behaviour at about 14.5 degrees. The project was graded 80%.

sections.heading: Method
body: I chose turbulence models against the near-wall resolution: RNG k-epsilon with wall functions on the coarse mesh, then Spalart-Allmaras once Fluent's Adapt function had resolved the viscous sublayer.
I checked Reynolds number similarity by scaling geometry and fluid properties together, and the non-dimensional coefficients held to within 0.6%.

sections.heading: Result
body: Lift matched NASA experimental data to within 1.6% and was stable to within 0.2% under grid refinement.
Drag shifted 25% with refinement because of near-wall sensitivity, and I gave three evidence-based reasons for the larger drag discrepancy against experiment.

sections.heading: Planned follow-up
body: Repeat the study in SU2 or OpenFOAM and compare the open-source results with Fluent. This is the first project on the simulation track.

title: H2OME: Mars Settlement Siting
summary: A hackathon entry (GirlsWhoML x PhysicsX) that sized a closed-loop household energy and water system and assessed candidate Mars sites with a Gaussian process model.

sections.heading: What I did
body: In a team of three I designed the household unit for a Mars settlement: solar power, battery storage, water electrolysis, a hydrogen fuel cell and a Sabatier reactor that recycles water.
I built an optimiser that sizes each site's solar array and battery to deliver 400 kWh per sol at 95% reliability, based on that site's own conditions rather than one fixed design.

sections.heading: Team result
body: With two teammates I built a Gaussian process model to assess thousands of candidate sites across 80 locations and 8 water-mining hubs. It found that hydrogen from the hubs extends habitation from about 55 to 84 degrees latitude.

sections.heading: What I learned
body: This was where I learned to work with AI coding tools, Claude Code and Cursor, to speed up iteration on the simulation workflow.

title: Battery Manufacturing Digital Twin
summary: A Python digital twin of an automotive battery production line, validated against experimental data to judge how far a virtual replica can be trusted.

sections.heading: What I did
body: I built a Python digital twin to analyse efficiency and operational performance across the production supply chain. The project was graded 82%.
I built the bill of materials for the line and analysed facility layouts using Industry 4.0 and continuous improvement principles, along with automation strategies to improve throughput.

sections.heading: Validation
body: Twin outputs were compared with experimental data using statistical analysis, to evaluate the accuracy and limits of virtual replication and support data-driven decisions on process improvement.

title: Heat Sink Performance Optimisation
summary: A multi-physics study of heat transfer, flow and thermal stress across heat sink configurations, with hand calculations checking the simulations.

sections.heading: What I did
body: I designed and analysed multi-physics models in ANSYS and MATLAB to evaluate heat transfer, flow behaviour and thermal stress across heat sink configurations. The project was graded 94%.
I used parametric modelling and optimisation to weigh structural against thermal trade-offs, validating each decision against performance targets.

sections.heading: Checks
body: Hand calculations supported the simulation findings and confirmed design margins across the configurations.
This connects directly to my Siemens work on electronics thermal management in Simcenter FLOEFD.

sections.heading: Planned follow-up
body: Train a surrogate model on this design space and report its error against the full simulation. This is the first project on the engineering and machine learning track.
